title: Playing a prismatic that rewards trait count

video.title: This Is Why You Always Take “Trait Ladder” on Set 18!

player.name: Dishsoap
player.about: Two-time World Champion and co-curator of TFT Academy. When he calls an augment an always-take, the game shows the conditions that make it one.

summary: Launch-patch game built around the prismatic augment Trait Ladder: a random emblem now, then a reward each time the board fields a rising number of different traits in a combat. Dishsoap shows how to build a board that keeps climbing the ladder.
thesis: An augment is only as good as the board that can use it, and Trait Ladder is the clearest case: its value is the number of distinct traits you can field, which favours flexible boards with many unique traits over verticals. The game is a study in reading an augment against the shop in front of you: which cheap units add a new trait, which emblems change the count, and when a stronger unit is the wrong buy because it duplicates a trait you already have.

timeline.title: Why this prismatic and not the others
timeline.watch: The two alternatives on offer and the board at 2-1. Trait Ladder gives an emblem immediately; note which unit gets it and whether that emblem adds a trait the board did not have.
timeline.why: The evaluation is strength now versus strength later against your HP and your board. A prismatic that starts paying in stage 2 is a different pick from one that pays at 5-1.
timeline.question: How many distinct traits can his stage-2 board field, and which shop unit would add one for the least gold?

timeline.title: Buying traits, not units
timeline.watch: Shop purchases that a normal board would skip: 1-costs bought for a trait they bring, not for their strength. Compare with the copies he does not buy because the trait is already covered.
timeline.why: Trait breakpoints, not unit cost, decide what a board does. With this augment the first breakpoint of many traits is worth more than the third breakpoint of one.

timeline.title: Level 6 buys a trait slot
timeline.watch: The level at 3-2 and what the sixth unit adds. Watch whether the level is taken before the augment rewards are counted for the round.
timeline.why: Each level is one more unit, and here one more unit is one more trait toward the next rung of the ladder; the level timing has a second payoff.

timeline.title: Items on the board, whatever the board is
timeline.watch: The first two completed items and who holds them. In a game where the units change often, note which items he chooses because they move well.
timeline.why: Two completed items by 3-2 is the rule regardless of the plan; tank items and most damage items transfer when the board changes.

timeline.title: The third augment against a board already built
timeline.watch: Whether the 4-2 pick adds combat strength or another emblem, and how it interacts with the ladder count.
timeline.why: The third augment is chosen with the most information; the right pick is the one that fixes what the board lacks at 4-2, not the highest-rated one.
timeline.question: What does the board lack at 4-2: frontline, damage, or one more trait? Which augment on offer fixes that?

timeline.title: Level 8 and the trait-per-slot trade
timeline.watch: How the roll at 8 is spent: 4-costs that both upgrade the board and add a trait versus stronger units that duplicate one.
timeline.why: Every slot has two values here, strength and trait count. The best buy maximises the sum, which is why the board ends up unusual.

timeline.title: Capping: when to stop climbing the ladder
timeline.watch: The point where he stops adding traits and starts two-starring carries or adding a 5-cost. Look at the reward sizes versus the fights he is winning.
timeline.why: The ladder pays less per rung relative to what a 2-star 4-cost adds late. Knowing when the augment has done its work is part of playing it.

questions.q: Why does Trait Ladder suit a flexible player more than a vertical player?
questions.a: Its rewards count distinct traits fielded in a combat. A vertical board stacks copies of one trait and fields few distinct ones; a flex board of one-of-each traits climbs the ladder faster and gets an emblem that adds another.

questions.q: What is the trap when playing this augment?
questions.a: Buying weak units for their traits so long that the board loses fights and bleeds HP. The rewards must convert into a board that wins; if the ladder is climbing while HP falls under 40 by 4-1, the augment is being played, not the game.

questions.q: How would you evaluate it at 2-1 with a board of two Defenders and a Rapidfire pair?
questions.a: Count the distinct traits you can reach at level 5 with cheap buys and one emblem; if it is five or more, the augment pays early and the pick is good. If the shop and the emblem push you into duplicates, a strength augment is the safer 2-1.

sourceNote: Title, channel, date and length come from the video page; the augment text (a random emblem, then rewards for fielding a rising number of non-unique traits) comes from the set data. The stage guide is TFT Lab's reading; the video has no creator chapters, so stops are anchored to stages.
